argument: The first line interpolates both points, so its nonnegative squared loss is zero and minimal. The others each have a nonzero residual; distinct x guarantees uniqueness.
The expression is at least 5 because the coefficient 2 is positive, and evaluating at m=3 attains 5. The alternatives are below the lower bound.
Substitution of the mean point into y=mx+p gives 10=6+p and hence p=4. The alternatives yield p=-17 or p=10 and fail the mean-point invariant.
The cross term in the centred expansion is 2q*sum(Yi-mXi)=0. Thus the only p-dependent term is n q² with n>0, uniquely minimised at q=0; individual residuals may remain nonzero.
Set q=2m+p; squared loss in q is sum(yi-ybar)²+n(q-ybar)². Therefore every and only pair with q=5 is optimal, producing infinitely many slope/intercept pairs.
The horizontal line y=4 has zero loss. With varying x, the coefficient Sxx is positive and the completed-square formula guarantees this parameter pair is unique.
For data y=2x with varying x, Sxy=2Sxx and Syy=4Sxx. The wrong ratio gives 1/2, while the exact zero-loss slope is 2, a direct implementation counterexample.
Subtracting the optimal loss from the loss at any m gives Sxx*(m-mstar)², positive whenever m differs from mstar. This proves uniqueness without assuming a zero residual fit.
